Intro.Title: What is FluentLocalizer?
Intro.Description: FluentLocalizer is a .NET library for building localized messages from templates, with arguments and grammar rules defined for each language.
Intro.Overview1: Localizing an application means providing labels, buttons, notifications and emails in several languages. Some messages also depend on data: *You have 1 message* and *You have 3 messages*, or *She replied* and *He replied*, need different wording.
Intro.Overview2: FluentLocalizer keeps messages in catalogs separate from your code, ready for review and translation. In your application, a fluent API lets you build a request for the user’s language:
Intro.Overview3: The templates contain the wording and the rules for plurals and gender. Your code supplies the key and data without choosing grammatical forms or concatenating sentence fragments.
Intro.ConceptsIntro: These five terms recur throughout the guides. Some describe localization concepts; others refer to library interfaces and types.
Intro.KeyText: The name of a message, such as `Inbox:Unread`. Your code refers to messages only by key. The `:` separates the parts of a key, so related messages can be grouped.
Intro.TemplateText: A message’s text, with placeholders for changing values and rules for plurals and variants. For example: `You have '{quantity, plural, one{# message} other{# messages}}'`. The [ICU message syntax](docs/templates) lets you define these rules in the template.
Intro.CultureText: The language and local conventions represented by `CultureInfo`. A .NET culture name can identify a language, such as `it`, or include a country or region, such as `it-CH`. It determines template selection and the formatting rules for numbers, dates and plurals.
Intro.StoreText: The component that retrieves templates from your translation source: JSON files, embedded resources, a web server or a database. Each store implements `ITranslationStore`, so you can change sources while keeping the same translation API.
Intro.TranslatorText: The service your code uses to obtain messages. `ITranslator.Get(key)` creates a request, you add its arguments, and `Resolve()` returns the formatted text. `Translator` is the implementation included in the library.
Intro.FlowTitle: What happens when you resolve a message
Intro.FlowIntro: Resolving a message involves these steps:
Intro.Flow1: `translator.Get(key)` creates a `TranslationBuilder` and captures `CultureInfo.CurrentUICulture`. The request retains that culture.
Intro.Flow2: You add the values the template needs with `WithArg`, `Pluralize` or `Genderize`. Optionally you choose a letter case with `WithCase`, or force another culture with `WithCulture`.
Intro.Flow3: `Resolve()` (or `ResolveAsync()`) asks the store for the template of that key in that culture. The store applies its own fallback rules: a JSON store, for example, looks for `it-CH`, then for `it`, then for your fallback language.
Intro.Flow4: [MessageFormat](https://github.com/jeffijoe/messageformat.net), Jeff Hansen’s open-source ICU implementation for .NET, formats the template using the supplied arguments and the requested culture’s plural, number and date rules.
Intro.Flow5: If the key does not exist or the template contains a mistake, `TranslationOptions` decide what you get back: a visible placeholder such as `[Inbox:Unread]`, a text of your choice, or an exception. See [Missing keys and errors](docs/errors).
Intro.PackagesIntro: FluentLocalizer is split into three NuGet packages, so an application only references what it uses:
Intro.CorePackage: The translator, the request builder, `TranslationOptions`, the store and logging interfaces. It contains no store.
Intro.CoreWhen: Always. The other two packages depend on it.
Intro.JsonPackage: Three ready-made stores for JSON catalogs: `JsonFileStore` (files on disk), `EmbeddedJsonStore` (files compiled into an assembly) and `HttpJsonStore` (files downloaded from a web server).
Intro.JsonWhen: When your translations are JSON files: the recommended way to start.
Intro.InjectionPackage: `AddFluentLocalizer()` for `IServiceCollection`, and an adapter that writes translation events to `ILogger`.
Intro.InjectionWhen: In ASP.NET Core, Blazor, worker services and any application that uses Microsoft dependency injection.
Intro.Platforms: The three packages always share the same version number and are released together. They target .NET Standard 2.0, .NET 8 and .NET 10, so they run on .NET Framework 4.7.2 and later, on every current version of .NET, and in the browser with Blazor WebAssembly (except `JsonFileStore`, which needs a file system).
Intro.Comparison1: The classic .NET approach stores fixed strings in `.resx` files and reads them with `ResourceManager` or `IStringLocalizer`. It works well for fixed labels, but it leaves three problems to your code:
Intro.Comparison2: *Plurals and gender.* A `.resx` file stores strings but does not define plural or select rules. Your code has to handle those rules, for example with `if` statements. FluentLocalizer puts them in each language’s template.
Intro.Comparison3: *Readable placeholders.* Composite formatting uses positions such as `'{0}'` and `'{1}'`, which say nothing to a translator. Templates use names such as `'{name}'` and `'{orderId}'`.
Intro.Comparison4: *Where the text lives.* Resources must be compiled into satellite assemblies. FluentLocalizer reads templates from any store: files that can be edited without recompiling, catalogs downloaded at runtime, or your own database.
Intro.NextQuickStartText: Follow a console example to install the packages and produce your first translated message.

QuickStart.Title: Quick start
QuickStart.Description: Install the packages, write your first JSON catalogs and show a translated message in a console application, one step at a time.
QuickStart.Before: You need the [.NET SDK](https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download), version 8 or later, and a terminal. This guide creates a console application named `HelloLocalizer`. For other project types, the same concepts apply with adjustments to the initial setup.
QuickStart.Install: The first package contains the translator. The second contains the stores that read JSON files.
QuickStart.Catalogs1: Create a folder called `Locales` in the project and add one JSON file per language. The file name is the culture name: `en.json` for English, `it.json` for Italian. Each property name is a key, and each text value is a template.
QuickStart.Catalogs2: `Greeting` is a top-level key. `Unread` is inside `Inbox`, so its key is `Inbox:Unread`. The placeholder `'{name}'` is replaced with the value supplied at runtime. The `plural` block chooses the wording by quantity: `=0` for zero, `one` for the singular category and `other` for the remaining cases. See [Writing templates](docs/templates) for details.

QuickStart.Copy2: Without this step the `Locales` folder does not exist at runtime. The store then finds no files and every message comes back as its key in brackets, such as `[Greeting]`. Set `ThrowOnMissingStore = true` in the store options to get an exception instead.
QuickStart.Code2: `JsonFileStore` reads the catalogs. `FallbackCulture = "en"` names the language used when the requested one has no file or no translation for a key.
QuickStart.Code3: `Translator` combines the store with the default options. Create it once and reuse it for the whole application.
QuickStart.Code4: `CultureInfo.CurrentUICulture` is the language of the user interface. Every request created afterwards uses it, both to choose the catalog and to format numbers and plurals.
QuickStart.Code5: `Get(key)` starts a request, `WithArg` fills `'{name}'`, `Pluralize(3)` gives the number to the `plural` block, and `Resolve()` returns the finished text.

QuickStart.Run2: Change `it-IT` to `en-US` and run the program again to use the English catalog. With `fr-FR`, there is no French catalog, so the store uses the English fallback. Try `Pluralize(0)` and `Pluralize(1)` to check the other template branches.
