Templates.Title: Writing templates
Templates.Description: ICU message syntax combines text, named placeholders and `plural` and `select` blocks. Numbers and dates are formatted using the request’s culture.
Templates.Placeholders1: A template contains text and *placeholders*. A name in braces, such as `'{name}'`, marks where the value of the `name` argument is inserted at runtime.
Templates.PlaceholderNames: Argument names are not case-sensitive: `'{Name}'` in the template and `WithArg("name", …)` in the code refer to the same argument.
Templates.PlaceholderRequired: Each placeholder needs a value in the request or in `DefaultArguments`. If the value is missing, formatting fails; with the default options, the result is `[Format Error]`. See [Missing keys and errors](docs/errors).
Templates.PlaceholderNull: A value of `null` is allowed and prints nothing.
Templates.PlaceholderValues: Values can be of any type. A plain placeholder converts them to text with the culture of the request: `1234.5` becomes `1234,5` in Italian and a `DateTime` uses that culture's date and time format. Plain placeholders do not add thousands separators: use `number` for that (see below).
Templates.PlaceholderSpaces: Spaces inside the braces are allowed: `'{ name }'` works like `'{name}'`.
Templates.Plural1: Plural rules vary by language. A `plural` block chooses the text using the supplied number and the rules of the request’s culture:
Templates.Plural2: The block starts with the name of the argument that holds the number (`quantity`), then the keyword `plural`, then a list of branches. Each branch is a selector followed by text in braces:
Templates.BranchCategories: Plural categories. Which ones a language uses, and for which numbers, is defined by the Unicode [CLDR plural rules](https://www.unicode.org/cldr/charts/latest/supplemental/language_plural_rules.html). Categories that a language does not use are simply never chosen.
Templates.BranchOther: Required. Used for every number that no other branch matches.
Templates.BranchExact: Matches exactly that number and wins over the categories. Typical use: `=0` for a *no messages* sentence.
Templates.BranchHash: Inside a branch, prints the number. It is printed as is, without culture formatting: `1234.5` stays `1234.5`. Write `'{quantity, number}'` instead of `#` to format it for the culture.
Templates.Plural3: Each translation lists the categories of its own language. For example:
Templates.PluralOther: Always write an `other` branch. If the number matches no branch and there is no `other`, formatting fails.
Templates.PluralQuantity: `Pluralize(3)` is a shortcut for `WithArg("quantity", 3)`, so it fills blocks that start with `'{quantity, plural, …}'`. A block can use any other argument name, set with `WithArg`: `'{count, plural, …}'` with `WithArg("count", 3)`.
Templates.PluralMissing: Every request starts with `quantity` set to `null`. If you forget `Pluralize`, the block treats the value as `0` and chooses the `=0` branch or the category of zero.
Templates.PluralValues: The value can be any number (`int`, `long`, `double`, `decimal`…) or a text that contains a number, such as `"3"`. `Pluralize` accepts only whole numbers: pass decimals with `WithArg("quantity", 1.5)`. A value that is not a number is a formatting error.
Templates.Offset: `offset:n` subtracts `n` from the number before choosing a category and before printing `#`. Exact branches such as `=1` still compare the original number. It is useful for sentences such as *You and 2 other people*:
Templates.Select1: A `select` block chooses a branch by comparing a text value with the branch names. It is the natural choice for gender, but it works for any fixed set of values: roles, statuses, product types.
Templates.SelectMatch: The comparison is exact and case-sensitive: the value `Female` does not match the branch `female`.
Templates.SelectOther: Write an `other` branch for values that match no branch: without it, an unknown value is a formatting error.
Templates.SelectGender: `Genderize(Gender.Female)` is a shortcut that sets the `gender` argument to `female`. The possible values are `unspecified`, `male`, `female` and `neuter`. Every request starts with `gender` set to `unspecified`, which falls into `other` unless the template has an `unspecified` branch.
Templates.SelectEnum: An `enum` passed with `WithArg` is compared by its name: `WithArg("status", Status.Active)` matches the branch `Active`.
Templates.Ordinal1: `selectordinal` works like `plural`, but uses the rules for positions in a sequence (1st, 2nd, 3rd) instead of quantities. English needs four branches; many languages need only `other`.
Templates.Formats1: A placeholder can name a format after the argument. The output follows the culture of the request:
Templates.FormatsCurrency: `currency` uses the currency of the culture, not of the amount: in `it-IT` every amount is shown in euros. When an application handles several currencies, format the amount in code and pass the text.
Templates.FormatsStyles: The supported styles are the ones in the table. Others, such as `date, long`, `time, full` or custom patterns like `dd/MM`, are not supported by MessageFormat and cause a formatting error.
Templates.FormatsPlain: `DateTime`, `DateTimeOffset` and `DateOnly` values work with `date`; `int`, `long`, `double` and `decimal` values work with `number`.
Templates.Nesting1: Blocks can be placed inside the branches of other blocks, and a template can span several lines. Put `select` outside and `plural` inside:
Templates.Nesting2: The order matters because `#` is replaced only directly inside a `plural` branch. In a `select` placed inside a `plural`, `#` stays a literal `#` character: there, write `'{quantity}'` instead.
Templates.Escaping1: Curly braces mark placeholders, so to show a brace as text, put it between apostrophes. The apostrophe is the escape character of the ICU syntax:
Templates.Escaping2: Two apostrophes in a row print one. A single apostrophe that is not followed by a brace (or by `#` inside a plural branch) is printed as is, so contractions and elisions such as *it's* or *l'utente* need no escaping. Backslashes have no special meaning: `\'{'` is a syntax error.
Templates.Special1: A few argument names behave in a special way:
Templates.SpecialBuiltIn: `quantity` and `gender` exist on every request, before you set anything: `quantity` is `null` and `gender` is `unspecified`. `Pluralize` and `Genderize` simply change them.
Templates.SpecialDefaults: Values for `quantity` and `gender` in `TranslationOptions.DefaultArguments` are not used because each request already defines them. Set these arguments on the request.
Templates.SpecialLength: `'{Length}'`: when a template contains exactly `'{Length}'` and the request has no argument called `Length`, FluentLocalizer fills it with the number of arguments whose value is not `null`. The count includes the built-in `gender` argument, so a request with one argument of your own produces `2`. Avoid the name, or set it yourself with `WithArg("Length", …)`.
Templates.Tip1: Write a complete sentence in each branch. Word order and agreement can change between languages, making concatenated fragments harder to translate.
Templates.Tip2: Use the same argument names in every language, and descriptive ones: `'{recipientName}'` tells a translator more than `'{n}'`.
Templates.Tip3: Store text in normal sentence case and apply `WithCase(LetterCase.Upper)` where the design needs capitals, as this site does for its small headings.
Templates.Tip4: In JSON catalogs, the template is a JSON string: quotes inside it are written `\"`, and the file must be saved as UTF-8.
Templates.Tip5: Try a template in the [playground](playground) before shipping it: it runs the same engine.
Templates.Reference: Templates are parsed and formatted by [MessageFormat](https://github.com/jeffijoe/messageformat.net), whose documentation describes every supported feature. The [ICU message formatting guide](https://unicode-org.github.io/icu/userguide/format_parse/messages/) describes the syntax in general.

Requests.Title: Building requests
Requests.Description: Use `Get(key)` to create a fluent builder and configure arguments, culture, letter case and options. `Resolve()` or `ResolveAsync()` retrieves the template and returns the formatted message.
Requests.Anatomy1: `Get(key)` returns a `TranslationBuilder`. Each `With…`, `Pluralize` and `Genderize` method updates that builder and returns the same instance, allowing you to chain calls. This is the *fluent* API pattern. `Resolve()` completes the request and returns a `string`.
Requests.Anatomy2: Nothing is looked up or formatted until `Resolve()` or `ResolveAsync()` is called. Until then the builder only collects settings, so the order of the calls between `Get` and `Resolve` does not matter.
Requests.Get: Defined on `ITranslator`. Creates a new builder for the key and records `CultureInfo.CurrentUICulture`. A `null` key throws `ArgumentNullException`; an empty key is passed to the store, which normally treats it as missing.
Requests.WithArg: Adds a named value, or replaces the value already set with the same name. Names are not case-sensitive. The value can be `null`; a `null` name throws `ArgumentNullException`.
Requests.WithArgs: Adds every entry of a `Dictionary<string, object?>`, exactly as if `WithArg` were called for each one. A `null` dictionary is ignored.
Requests.Pluralize: Sets the `quantity` argument, used by `'{quantity, plural, …}'` blocks. Accepts an `int`; for other numbers use `WithArg("quantity", value)`.
Requests.Genderize: Sets the `gender` argument to the lowercase name of a `Gender` value: `unspecified`, `male`, `female` or `neuter`. Used by `'{gender, select, …}'` blocks.
Requests.WithCase: Chooses a transformation of the letter case, applied to the finished text. See [Letter case](docs/requests#letter-case) below.
Requests.WithCulture: Forces a culture for this request only, instead of the one recorded by `Get`. Accepts a `CultureInfo` or a name such as `"it-IT"`; an unknown name throws `CultureNotFoundException`. See [Choosing the culture](docs/culture).
Requests.WithOptions: Replaces the translator's `TranslationOptions` for this request only. Passing `null` restores the default options. See [Missing keys and errors](docs/errors#per-request).
Requests.Resolve: Asks the store for the template synchronously, formats it and returns the text.
Requests.ResolveAsync: Asks the store for the template asynchronously, then formats it. Use it with stores that download or read data asynchronously.
Requests.MethodsOrder: Calling a method twice keeps the last value: `.Pluralize(1).Pluralize(5)` uses `5`.
Requests.Arguments1: Each request combines two sets of values: the `DefaultArguments` of `TranslationOptions`, shared by every request, and the values set on the request itself.
Requests.ArgumentsReplace: A value set on the request always replaces a default with the same name, regardless of upper or lower case.
Requests.ArgumentsDefaults: Defaults are useful for values that appear in many templates, such as the product name or a support address. They cannot provide `quantity` or `gender`, which every request already defines.
Requests.ArgumentsUnused: Arguments that the template does not use are simply ignored. A placeholder without a value, on the other hand, is a formatting error.
Requests.Case1: `WithCase` changes the letters of the finished message. The table shows the result for the text `hello WORLD fooBar 42abc`:
Requests.CaseAfter: The transformation is applied after formatting, to the whole message, including the values of the arguments.
Requests.CaseInvariant: `Upper` and `Lower` use the invariant culture rules, not those of the request: the Turkish dotted and dotless *i*, for example, are not handled. All other characters, accented letters included, are converted normally.
Requests.CaseWords: `CamelCase`, `PascalCase`, `SnakeCase` and `KebabCase` split the text into words at spaces, punctuation, changes from lower to upper case and changes between letters and digits, then join the words again. Spaces and punctuation are removed, so these four are meant for identifiers (CSS classes, file names, URL segments), not for sentences.
Requests.Sync: `Resolve()` is the simplest choice, and the one to use in Razor markup. It works with every store that can answer immediately: `JsonFileStore`, `EmbeddedJsonStore`, an in-memory store, and `HttpJsonStore` after its catalogs have been loaded with `LoadAsync`.
Requests.Async: `ResolveAsync()` calls the store's asynchronous method and passes it the optional `CancellationToken`, so a store that downloads files can stop when the operation is canceled. Formatting itself is always synchronous and very fast. With stores that keep everything in memory the two methods give the same result.
Requests.Implicit1: A builder converts itself to a `string` automatically, and its `ToString()` method returns the resolved text. Both call `Resolve()`. This is what makes `@Translator.Get("Home:Title")` work in Razor and lets you pass a builder where a `string` is expected:
Requests.Implicit2: Each conversion resolves the message again. Store the `string` in a variable if you need it several times. Serializers such as `System.Text.Json` do not call `ToString()`: resolve the text before putting it in an object that will be serialized, for example when sending labels to JavaScript.
Requests.LifetimeTranslator: `Translator` keeps no state of its own besides the store, the options and the logger: create it once and share it for the whole application, from any thread. With dependency injection it is a singleton.
Requests.LifetimeBuilder: `TranslationBuilder` is mutable and not thread-safe. Create a new one for each message with `Get(key)`, and do not share it between threads or store it for later: it keeps the culture recorded when it was created, even after the application changes language.
Requests.LifetimeRepeat: A builder can be resolved more than once; each call asks the store again and formats the template again.
Requests.LifetimeOptions: The translator keeps a reference to its `TranslationOptions`, not a copy. Changing a property of that object later affects every request created afterwards; to avoid surprises, configure the options before creating the translator and leave them unchanged.
Requests.DirectTitle: Creating a builder without a translator
Requests.Direct1: `TranslationBuilder` has a public constructor, so code that only has a store can create a request directly. Its parameters mirror what `Translator` passes:
Requests.Direct2: `Translator.Get(key)` does exactly this with its own store, options and logger. Prefer `ITranslator` in application code: it can be injected and replaced in tests.

Culture.Title: Choosing the culture
Culture.Description: Requests use the interface language through `CurrentUICulture`. Set it when your application selects the user’s language; use `WithCulture` for messages that need a different culture.
Culture.Basics1: In .NET a language is represented by a `CultureInfo` object, identified by a name. A *neutral* culture names only a language; a *specific* culture adds a country or region, which can change spelling, vocabulary and the way numbers and dates are written:
Culture.Name: Name
Culture.ItNeutral: Italian, in general. It is the *parent* of every specific Italian culture.
Culture.ItItaly: Italian as used in Italy: decimal comma, `1.234,5`.
Culture.ItSwitzerland: Italian as used in Switzerland: apostrophe as thousands separator, `1’234.5`.
Culture.Basics2: Every thread of a .NET application has two current cultures:
Culture.UiCulture: `CultureInfo.CurrentUICulture`, the language of the user interface. .NET uses it to choose resources, and FluentLocalizer uses it for translations.
Culture.FormatCulture: `CultureInfo.CurrentCulture`, the conventions for formatting. .NET uses it in `ToString()`, `string.Format` and string interpolation.
Culture.Basics3: FluentLocalizer reads only `CurrentUICulture`, and uses it for both jobs inside a template: choosing the template and formatting numbers, dates and plurals. To keep the rest of your application consistent, set both cultures to the same value.
Culture.Default1: You normally never pass a culture to FluentLocalizer. Set `CurrentUICulture` where your application decides the user's language, and every request follows it:
Culture.Default2: The culture is read once, when `Get(key)` creates the request, and kept by that request. A request created before a language change keeps the old language:
Culture.Default3: So after changing language, create new requests. Text that was already shown, such as a rendered page or a value stored in a field, is not updated by itself: the code that owns it must render it again.
Culture.OverrideTitle: Choose a culture for one request
Culture.Override1: `WithCulture(...)` is for the exceptions: messages that must not follow the user interface, such as an email in the recipient's language, a document generated for another country, or a page that shows the same text in several languages side by side.
Culture.OverrideScope: It affects only that request, for choosing the template and for formatting. It never changes `CurrentUICulture` or `CurrentCulture`.
Culture.OverrideName: `WithCulture("it-IT")` accepts a culture name; an unknown name throws `CultureNotFoundException`.
Culture.OverrideNull: `WithCulture((CultureInfo)null)` does not restore the UI culture: it selects `CurrentCulture`, the formatting culture. Avoid passing `null`.
Culture.OverrideTip: If all requests should use the same culture, set `CurrentUICulture` rather than repeating `WithCulture(...)`. New requests will then follow subsequent language changes.
Culture.AppsTitle: Setting the culture in your application
Culture.Console: Set the two cultures at startup, before creating any request. The `DefaultThread…` properties give the same culture to threads that start later and have not set their own:
Culture.AspNet1: A server works for many users at once, each with their own language. The request localization middleware chooses a culture for each HTTP request (from the query string, a cookie or the `Accept-Language` header) and sets both current cultures for it:
Culture.AspNet2: Do not change `DefaultThreadCurrentUICulture` per user in a server: it is shared by the whole process. The current cultures set by the middleware belong to each request.
Culture.Blazor1: In the browser there is one user, so set the default thread cultures before starting the application:
Culture.Blazor2: To change language while the application runs, assign the new culture to the same properties and render the components again: components show text resolved during their last render. This site passes the culture to its pages as a cascading value, so changing the language re-renders every page that receives it. The browser also needs the formatting data of every language you offer; if you switch between several languages, add this to the project file:
Culture.AsyncFlow: The current cultures are part of the execution context: on modern .NET they flow across `await`, `Task.Run` and other task-based code, so an asynchronous method keeps the culture of the code that called it.
Culture.Fallback1: Choosing the template when the requested language is not available is the store's job. The JSON stores, for example, look for `it-CH`, then for `it`, then for their `FallbackCulture`, one key at a time: [JSON stores](docs/stores/json#fallback) describes the exact rules. A custom store applies the rules you write.
Culture.Fallback2: Even when the template comes from the fallback language, it is formatted with the culture of the request. An English template served to a German request prints `1.234,5` instead of `1,234.5`, and its `plural` block uses the German plural rules: keep the `other` branch in every template so any language finds a match.

Errors.Title: Missing keys and errors
Errors.Description: Configure what happens when a translation is missing or formatting fails: return a visible placeholder, return fallback text or throw an exception.
Errors.Kinds1: When `Resolve()` cannot produce a message, the cause belongs to one of three groups. The first two are handled by `TranslationOptions`; the third always reaches your code.
Errors.MissingCauses: The store returns `null`, an empty text or a text made only of spaces, or throws `KeyNotFoundException`. Usually a key that does not exist in any language, or a typo in the key.
Errors.FormatCauses: The template has a syntax error (an unclosed brace), a placeholder has no value, a `plural` value is not a number, no branch matches and there is no `other`, or a format style is not supported.
Errors.StoreCauses: Anything else the store throws: a file that cannot be read, a network error, a missing catalog when the store is configured to throw, a canceled operation.
Errors.StoreHandled: Nobody: the exception propagates unchanged to the caller of `Resolve()`.
Errors.Defaults1: For missing translations and formatting errors, the default options return a placeholder instead of throwing an exception. Store errors still propagate to the caller:
Errors.DefaultsMissing: A missing translation returns the key in square brackets: `[Inbox:Unread]`.
Errors.Defaults2: An empty text in a catalog counts as missing, not as a valid translation: it produces `[key]` and does not fall back to another language. To fall back, remove the key from the catalog.
Errors.Options1: Pass a `TranslationOptions` object to the translator to change these rules for every request. All properties can be set at any time, but set them before creating the translator: the translator keeps a reference to the object, not a copy.
Errors.OptMissingBehavior: What a missing translation returns. See the table below.
Errors.OptMissingValue: The text returned with `ReturnConfiguredValue`. Supports the tokens described below. Ignored by `ReturnPlaceholder`, which always returns `[key]`.
Errors.OptMissingFactory: Creates the exception thrown with `ThrowException`. Receives the key and the culture.
Errors.OptFormatBehavior: What a formatting error returns. See the table below.
Errors.OptFormatValue: The text returned for a formatting error with `ReturnPlaceholder`. Supports the tokens described below.
Errors.OptFormatFactory: Creates the exception thrown for a formatting error with `ThrowException`. Receives the key and the culture.
Errors.OptDefaultArguments: Values available to every template, merged with the values of each request. The request's values win. Values for `quantity` and `gender` are ignored.
Errors.ConfiguredFormat: Not available: formatting errors have only the two other values.
Errors.ThrowMissing: Throws the exception created by `MissingKeyExceptionFactory`, or a `TranslationException`.
Errors.ThrowFormat: Throws the exception created by `FormattingErrorExceptionFactory`, or a `TranslationException`.
Errors.Tokens1: `MissingKeyFallbackValue` and `FormattingErrorFallbackValue` can contain tokens that are replaced with details of the failed request:
Errors.TokenCulture: The name of the request's culture, such as `it-IT`.
Errors.Tokens2: Tokens are replaced as plain text, ignoring upper and lower case (`'{KEY}'` works too). Fallback texts are not ICU templates: they cannot contain `plural` blocks or the request's arguments.
Errors.Exceptions1: With `ThrowException`, the default exception is a `TranslationException`. Besides the message, it carries the `Key` and the `Culture` of the request:
Errors.ExceptionsMissing: For a missing translation the message is *Unable to resolve translation key '…' for culture '…'*.
Errors.ExceptionsFormat: For a formatting error the message is *Unable to format translation '…' for culture '…'*, followed by the formatter's explanation, for example *The variable 'name' was not found in the arguments collection*. The original exception is described in the message but not attached as `InnerException`.
Errors.ExceptionsEmptyKey: A key that is empty or made only of spaces cannot become a `TranslationException`: with `ThrowException`, it throws `ArgumentException` instead.
Errors.Factories1: Set a factory to throw your own exception type. Each factory receives the key and the culture (which can be `null`):
Errors.FactoriesType: The exception returned by the factory is thrown as it is, whatever its type.
Errors.FactoriesNull: The missing-key factory must not return `null`. If the formatting factory returns `null`, the exception of a missing translation is used instead: the missing-key factory's, or a `TranslationException` with the *Unable to resolve* message.
Errors.FactoriesErrors: An exception thrown inside a factory propagates to the caller.
Errors.Helpers: `CreateMissingKeyException(key, culture)` and `CreateFormattingException(key, culture, innerException)` return the exception that the options would throw, without throwing it. They are useful in custom stores or tests that want the same exceptions as the translator. Both reject an empty key with `ArgumentException`.
Errors.PerRequest1: `WithOptions(...)` replaces the translator's options for a single request:
Errors.PerRequest2: The options are replaced as a whole, `DefaultArguments` included: copy the values you still need into the new object. `WithOptions(null)` restores the defaults.
Errors.RecommendDevelopment: *During development*, the default placeholders make a missing key obvious on screen. Switch `FormattingErrorBehavior` to `ThrowException` to see the formatter's explanation instead of `[Format Error]`.
Errors.RecommendTests: *In tests*, resolve every key in every language with both behaviors set to `ThrowException`, so a missing translation or a broken template fails the build. This site's test suite does exactly that for its own catalogs.
Errors.RecommendProduction: *In production*, choose fallback behavior to suit the message. For interface labels, fallback text may be preferable to an exception. `ReturnConfiguredValue` with an empty string hides a missing label; a placeholder makes the problem visible. Check that the choice is appropriate for the context.
Errors.RecommendLogging: *Always*, connect a logger: every fallback is logged as a warning with the key and the culture. See [Logging](docs/logging).

Logging.Title: Logging
Logging.Description: Log the translator’s lookups, fallbacks and errors. Use the single-method `ITranslationLogger` interface or integrate with .NET’s `ILogger`.
Logging.Interface1: Logging is optional and off by default. The core package defines a minimal interface in the `FluentLocalizer.Logging` namespace, so it does not depend on any logging library:
Logging.Interface2: Implement it and pass the logger as the third argument of `Translator`. A simple logger that writes warnings and errors to the console:
Logging.Events1: Only the translator writes to the logger, while it resolves a request. Stores do not log. The entries are:
Logging.DebugWhen: Every request: start, template received (only with `ResolveAsync`), formatting, completion.
Logging.DebugMessages: *Resolving translation request for key 'Inbox:Unread' for culture 'it-IT'.* and similar.
Logging.WarningWhen: A fallback text is returned instead of the message, for a missing translation or a formatting error.
Logging.WarningMessages: *Translation key '…' could not be resolved for culture '…'. Returning fallback value '[…]'.* or *Formatting failed for translation key '…'…*
Logging.ErrorWhen: Just before an exception leaves `Resolve()`: a missing translation or formatting error with `ThrowException`, or an exception thrown by the store. The exception is attached.
Logging.ErrorMessages: The same texts as the warnings, or *An unexpected exception occurred while resolving translation key '…'.*
Logging.UnusedWhen: Never used by the library. They exist so that adapters can map every level of their logging system.
Logging.EventsVolume: Debug entries are written for every message the application shows: enable them only while investigating a problem.
Logging.EventsFormatting: The warning for a formatting error does not include the formatter's explanation. To read it, use `FormattingErrorBehavior.ThrowException` while developing: the exception message contains it.
Logging.EventsTwice: When an exception factory returns an exception that is not a `TranslationException`, the error is logged twice: once when it is created and once as an unexpected exception.
Logging.ILogger1: With the dependency injection package, `WithLogger()` connects FluentLocalizer to the `ILogger` infrastructure of ASP.NET Core and of the .NET generic host, so translation events go wherever your other logs go (console, files, Application Insights, Serilog...):
Logging.ILoggerLevels: Each `TranslationLogLevel` is mapped to the `LogLevel` with the same name, and the text is logged as the structured property `Message`. Disabled levels are skipped.
Logging.ILoggerRequired: `WithLogger()` needs logging services in the container. Web and generic hosts register them for you; with a bare `ServiceCollection`, call `services.AddLogging()` first.
Logging.ILogger2: Filter the entries like any other category. This configuration keeps warnings and errors and hides the per-request debug entries:
Logging.Adapter: The adapter used by `WithLogger()` is internal. Without dependency injection, implement `ITranslationLogger` and forward its events to an `ILogger`:

Injection.Title: Dependency injection
Injection.Description: Register the translator once with Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection and inject `ITranslator` wherever you need text: controllers, Razor components, background services.
Injection.Install1: Add the integration package and the package of the store you use:
Injection.Install2: `AddFluentLocalizer` is declared in the `Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection` namespace, which ASP.NET Core and worker projects already import, so it needs no extra `using`. The builder it returns, `FluentLocalizerBuilder`, lives in the `FluentLocalizer.Core` namespace: you only need it if you write its type name.
Injection.Register1: One chain of calls in `Program.cs` registers everything:
Injection.RegisterStep1: `AddFluentLocalizer(...)` registers `ITranslator` and configures `TranslationOptions`. The callback is optional.
Injection.RegisterStep2: `WithStore(...)` registers the store. It is required: the translator cannot work without one.
Injection.RegisterStep3: `WithLogger()` is optional and sends translation events to `ILogger`. See [Logging](docs/logging).
Injection.ServiceTranslator: Registered by `AddFluentLocalizer`. A `Translator` built from the registered store, the options and the logger, if there is one.
Injection.ServiceOptions: Registered by `AddFluentLocalizer` through the standard options infrastructure.
Injection.ServiceLogger: Registered by `WithLogger`, as an adapter to `ILogger<Translator>`. Optional.
Injection.RegisteredLazy: The translator is created the first time something asks for it, and then shared: it is a singleton, like the store.
Injection.RegisteredNoStore: Without a registered store, the first request for `ITranslator` throws `InvalidOperationException` (*No service for type 'FluentLocalizer.ITranslationStore'*).
Injection.RegisteredOwn: `WithStore` and `WithLogger` are shortcuts. Registering your own `ITranslationStore` or `ITranslationLogger` with `services.AddSingleton<…>(…)` works the same way.
Injection.RegisteredTwice: Call `AddFluentLocalizer` once per container. A second call adds a second translator registration, and the container then returns the last one registered.
Injection.OptionsCallback: With a callback, the options are configured through the standard `IOptions<TranslationOptions>` pattern. Other `Configure<TranslationOptions>(...)` calls, in any order, are combined with it.
Injection.OptionsInstance: With a `TranslationOptions` object, that exact object is used, and other `Configure` calls are ignored. Passing `null` throws `ArgumentNullException`.
Injection.OptionsOnce: Either way, the options are read once, when the translator is created. Later changes to the configuration are not picked up while the application runs.
Injection.Options2: In ASP.NET Core and in the generic host, the simple properties can also come from `appsettings.json`. The exception factories and `DefaultArguments` must be set in code:
Injection.StoreTitle: Creating the store: instance or factory
Injection.Store1: `WithStore` accepts a store you have already created, or a function that creates it. The difference is who creates the store and who disposes of it:
Injection.InstanceDisposed: By you: the container does not dispose of objects it did not create.
Injection.FactoryCreated: By the container, the first time the store is needed.
Injection.FactoryDisposed: By the container, when the application stops, if the store implements `IDisposable` (as `JsonFileStore` and `HttpJsonStore` do).
Injection.Store2: Prefer the factory: the store is disposed of correctly, and the factory can use other services, such as the host environment or an `HttpClient`:
Injection.Consume1: Ask for `ITranslator` in the constructor of any registered class:
Injection.Consume2: In Blazor, inject it once for every component in `_Imports.razor`, then use it directly in the markup. Razor converts the request to text by itself, so `Resolve()` is not needed:
Injection.Consume3: A component shows the text it resolved during its last render. When the language changes, the component must render again: see [Choosing the culture](docs/culture#applications).
Injection.Blazor: Blazor WebAssembly usually reads its catalogs over HTTP, and preloads them before the first render: [HttpJsonStore](docs/stores/json/http#example) contains a complete `Program.cs`. For small catalogs embedded in the application, see [EmbeddedJsonStore](docs/stores/json/embedded#example), which this site uses.

Stores.Title: Stores
Stores.Description: A store retrieves templates from your translation source. Choose a built-in implementation or create your own; `ITranslationStore` provides a consistent interface for accessing templates.
Stores.Role1: A store answers a single question: *what is the template of this key in this culture?* Every store implements the `ITranslationStore` interface of the core package, with one synchronous and one asynchronous method:
Stores.RoleRaw: Returns the original template with its placeholders and ICU blocks. Substituting arguments and formatting the message are the translator’s responsibility.
Stores.RoleFallback: It decides what to do when the culture has no translation: look in a related language, in a fallback language, or nowhere. Fallback rules belong to the store.
Stores.RoleMissing: It returns `null` when it has no template for the key. The translator then applies the missing-translation rules of [TranslationOptions](docs/errors).
Stores.Role2: Because the translator only sees this interface, you can start with JSON files and move to another store later without changing the code that shows text.
Stores.Available1: These stores are ready to use. Each one has its own page with installation, options, behavior and error handling:
Stores.EmbeddedReads: JSON files compiled into an assembly
Stores.HttpReads: JSON files on a web server
Stores.Available2: *Browser* means Blazor WebAssembly and other applications running in the browser, which have no file system. *Namespace files* are the optional extra files that split a catalog by feature, described in [JSON stores](docs/stores/json#namespaces). New stores will be added to this list as they are released.
Stores.ChooseFile: *Server, console, desktop and worker applications*, where the translations are deployed as files next to the program and may be edited without recompiling: `JsonFileStore`. Start here if unsure.
Stores.ChooseEmbedded: *Libraries that ship their own texts, single-file applications, and Blazor WebAssembly applications with small catalogs*, where nothing should be deployed separately: `EmbeddedJsonStore`.
Stores.ChooseHttp: *Blazor WebAssembly and other client applications with large catalogs*, or translations that must change without publishing a new version: `HttpJsonStore` downloads only the languages and sections in use.
Stores.ChooseCustom: *Translations kept in a database, a CMS or a translation service*, or existing resources you want to reuse: a [custom store](docs/stores/custom).
Stores.Choosing2: The three JSON stores read the same files, so moving from one to another is a matter of changing a few lines at startup.
Stores.Families1: A *family* groups stores that read the same format and share key and fallback rules. The family page covers these rules; individual store pages explain loading, configuration and differences in behavior.
Stores.JsonFamilyText: Catalog format, namespaces, culture matching and fallback shared by JsonFileStore, EmbeddedJsonStore and HttpJsonStore.
Stores.CustomFamilyText: Implement ITranslationStore for any other source, combine stores, or build on the JSON infrastructure.
Stores.LifetimeOnce: Create one store for the whole application and share it. The JSON stores read and parse their files once and then keep them in memory: creating a store for every request would repeat that work each time.
Stores.LifetimeThreads: A store is used by every request, from any thread at the same time. All the stores of the library are thread-safe, and a custom store must be too.
Stores.LifetimeDispose: `JsonFileStore` and `HttpJsonStore` implement `IDisposable`. Release their resources when no longer needed using `using` or by letting the dependency injection container manage their lifetime. `EmbeddedJsonStore` owns no disposable resources and has no `Dispose()` method.

Json.Title: JSON stores
Json.Description: JSON stores share the catalog format, key and namespace rules, culture selection and fallback. This page covers those rules and the settings common to all three implementations.
Json.Family1: The `FluentLocalizer.Store.Json` package contains three stores, all in the `FluentLocalizer.Store.Json` namespace. Each store has its own options class, which inherits the settings shared by the family:
Json.FileBest: Servers, console, desktop and worker applications.
Json.EmbeddedBest: Libraries, single-file deployments, small Blazor WebAssembly apps.
Json.HttpBest: Blazor WebAssembly and clients that download translations.
Json.Family2: Everything on this page applies to all three stores, unless a difference is stated. The page of each store covers its setup, its own options and its specific behavior.
Json.Format1: A catalog is a JSON file with the translations of one culture. Its properties form the keys, and its text values are the templates:
Json.Format2: This file defines four keys: `Welcome`, `Checkout:Title`, `Checkout:Items` and `Checkout:Buttons:Pay`. A key is the path through the nested objects, with `:` between the names. The rules:
Json.RuleRoot: The root of the file must be an object.
Json.RuleNest: Always nest objects. The key is split at every `:`, so a property literally named `"Checkout:Title"` is never found. Nesting can go as deep as you need.
Json.RuleCase: Property names are case-sensitive: the key `checkout:title` does not find `Checkout:Title`.
Json.RuleSpaces: Spaces around the parts of a key and empty parts are ignored: `Checkout : Title` and `Checkout::Title` both find `Checkout:Title`.
Json.RuleDot: The dot has no special meaning in a key: `"Home.Title"` is a single property, reached with the key `Home.Title`.
Json.RuleStrings: Only text values are templates. A key that ends on a number, `true`/`false`, an array, `null` or an object counts as missing.
Json.RuleEmpty: An empty text, or a text made only of spaces, is returned by the store but treated as missing by the translator: it shows `[key]` and does not fall back to another language. Remove the key to let the fallback work.
Json.RuleSyntax: The files must be strict JSON: comments and trailing commas are not allowed. `JsonFileStore` and `EmbeddedJsonStore` ignore a file with a syntax error as a whole, unless `ThrowOnMissingStore` is enabled; `HttpJsonStore` always throws. See the table below.
Json.RuleEncoding: Save the files as UTF-8. Templates follow the [ICU syntax](docs/templates), and inside JSON strings quotes are written `\"`.
Json.Namespaces1: The first part of a key that has two or more parts is its *namespace*: in `common:Buttons:Save` the namespace is `common`. The namespace can stay in the culture file as a top-level object, or move to a file of its own, without the namespace object. The key is the same in both cases:
Json.Namespaces2: Namespace files split a large catalog by feature or by team, and let `HttpJsonStore` download only the sections a page uses. Moving a namespace from one place to the other requires no change in the code. These file names are recognized, shown for `it` and identical for a specific culture such as `it-IT`:
Json.NamespacesSupport: `JsonFileStore` and `HttpJsonStore` read all four kinds of file. `EmbeddedJsonStore` reads only culture files: keep namespaces as top-level objects when you embed the catalogs.
Json.NamespacesAny: Every key with at least two parts has a namespace, so `Checkout:Title` can also move to `it.Checkout.json` as `'{ "Title": "Il tuo carrello" }'`. The namespace file is tried first; a key not found there is still looked for in the culture file.
Json.NamespacesFolders: Culture folders are one level deep: files in deeper subfolders are not recognized automatically, but can be used through `FileMappings`.
Json.NamespacesCase: On case-sensitive file systems (Linux) and web servers, write culture names with the standard .NET spelling (`it-IT`, not `it-it`) and the namespace exactly as it appears in the keys: the stores build file names that way.
Json.Culture1: When a request arrives for a culture, the store must decide which files belong to it. The stores use one of two strategies, depending on whether they know the list of available files.
Json.KnowTitle: Stores that know the file list
Json.Know1: `JsonFileStore` scans its folder when it is created, and `HttpJsonStore` reads the list from an optional `manifest.json`. Both look at the culture names in the file names and choose, in this order:
Json.KnowExact: The exact culture, if it has files: `it-CH` for `it-CH`.
Json.KnowNeutral: For a specific culture, its neutral culture: `it` for `it-CH`.
Json.KnowRegional: For a neutral culture, the first specific culture of that language in alphabetical order: `it` with only `it-IT` files uses `it-IT`.
Json.KnowSibling: If only *other* specific cultures of the same language exist, such as `it-IT` for an `it-CH` request, the store throws `FileNotFoundException`: it never chooses a regional variant of the same language by itself.
Json.KnowNone: If the language has no files at all, the request goes directly to the fallback culture.
Json.Guess1: `EmbeddedJsonStore`, and `HttpJsonStore` without a manifest, do not know which files exist. They try the file names of the requested culture and of its language, `it-CH.json` and then `it.json`, and move on to the fallback culture if neither exists. They never discover `it-IT.json` for an `it` or `it-CH` request.
Json.SiblingWarning: The same rules choose the files of `FallbackCulture`. With `JsonFileStore`, a fallback of `en-US` and only an `en-GB.json` file, *every* request that needs the fallback throws `FileNotFoundException`. Make sure the fallback culture, or its neutral culture, has its own file. The exception is thrown whatever the value of `ThrowOnMissingStore`.
Json.Culture2: The neutral culture is normally the two-letter language code: `it`, `en`, `fr`. A few languages, such as Chinese, have intermediate cultures with a script (`zh-TW` belongs to `zh-Hant`), and the two strategies above treat them differently. For those cultures, point to the right file explicitly with `FileMappings`.
Json.FallbackTitle: Fallback, one key at a time
Json.Fallback1: For the key `common:Buttons:Save` requested in `it-CH`, a store tries these sources in order and returns the first text it finds:
Json.Fallback2: the file mapped to `it-CH` in `FileMappings`, if any;
Json.Fallback3: the `common` namespace files of `it-CH`, then the `it-CH` culture file;
Json.Fallback4: the same files for the neutral culture `it`;
Json.Fallback5: the same files for `FallbackCulture` and for its neutral culture.
Json.Fallback6: Fallback works per key, not per file: a key missing from `it-CH.json` is still found in `it.json` or in the fallback language. Regional and namespace files therefore only need the strings that differ.
Json.Fallback7: `EmbeddedJsonStore` follows the same order without namespace files. `HttpJsonStore` with a manifest follows it among the files the manifest lists, starting from the culture chosen as described above.
Json.Layout1: Name the main catalog of each language after its neutral culture, and add regional files only for the strings that differ. Set the fallback to a neutral culture with a complete catalog:
Json.Layout2: With this layout every store gives the same results: `it-IT`, `it-CH` and `it` read `it.json`; `en-GB` reads `en-GB.json` and then `en.json`; any other language reads `en.json`. This site uses the same layout: `en.json`, `it.json`, `fr.json`, `de.json` and `es.json`, with `FallbackCulture` set to `en`.
Json.Mappings1: `FileMappings` assigns a specific file to a culture. Use it to select another regional variant’s catalog, retain existing file names or handle cultures with a script:
Json.MappingsKeys: Keys are culture names, compared without regard to case.
Json.MappingsValues: For `JsonFileStore` and `HttpJsonStore`, values are relative paths of `.json` files inside the store's folder or URL path. Absolute paths, `..`, `.` and empty segments, `:`, `?` and `#` are rejected with `ArgumentException` when the store is created (by `HttpJsonStore` also `%`). For `EmbeddedJsonStore` the value is the final file name alone, such as `it-IT.json`, because embedded files are identified by that name.
Json.MappingsFirst: The mapped file is the first file tried for that culture; the usual file names follow.
Json.MappingsWhole: A mapped file is read as a culture file: it must contain the namespaces as top-level objects. `JsonFileStore` and `HttpJsonStore` with a manifest consider the culture available only if the mapped file exists.
Json.Settings1: `JsonStoreSettings` is the base class of the three options classes. Its properties are available on every JSON store:
Json.SettingFallback: The culture used when the requested one has no translation for a key. Must be a valid .NET culture name, and should have its own file (see the warning above).
Json.SettingMappings: Culture-to-file mappings, described above. The dictionary itself cannot be replaced: add entries to it.
Json.SettingThrow: Whether missing or unreadable catalogs throw exceptions instead of being skipped. Details in the next table.
Json.SettingMax: Maximum size in bytes of a single JSON file. `0` means no limit. Set it when the catalogs do not come from a trusted source. A negative value throws `ArgumentOutOfRangeException` when the store is created.
Json.NoFiles: No catalog at all (missing folder, no resources)
Json.NoFilesTrue: `FileNotFoundException` when the store is created (file and embedded) or on the first lookup (HTTP).
Json.InvalidFalse: File and embedded: the file is ignored. HTTP: `JsonException`.
Json.InvalidTrue: `JsonException`. `JsonFileStore` and `EmbeddedJsonStore` read and check every file when they are created, so the problem appears at startup.
Json.NoCulture: Neither the requested culture nor the fallback has any file
Json.MissingKey: The files exist but do not contain the key
Json.MissingKeyBoth: Always a missing translation (`null`), never an exception. The translator applies `TranslationOptions`.
Json.TooLargeBoth: Always an exception: `InvalidDataException` for file and embedded stores, `HttpRequestException` for HTTP.
Json.Sibling: Only a regional variant of the same language exists
Json.SiblingBoth: Always `FileNotFoundException`, in the stores that know the file list (see above).
Json.Settings2: Exceptions thrown by a store are not converted by the translator: they reach the caller of `Resolve()` or `ResolveAsync()`. Use `ThrowOnMissingStore = true` when a missing catalog is a deployment mistake that should stop the application at startup.
Json.SecurityData: Treat catalogs as part of the deployment, like code: whoever can change them can change what users read.
Json.SecurityHtml: The stores return plain text. Display it through your UI framework's normal text output, which escapes HTML, and never insert it as raw markup.
Json.SecuritySize: A very large or deeply nested catalog can consume memory and time. If catalogs can come from outside, set `MaxDocumentBytes` and limit response sizes on the server.
Json.SecurityPaths: File names built from keys and mappings are validated so they cannot leave the configured folder or URL path. `JsonFileStore` also refuses symbolic links: see its page.

JsonFile.Title: JsonFileStore
JsonFile.Description: `JsonFileStore` loads JSON catalogs from a directory on disk. Use it in server, console, desktop and worker applications; `ReloadOnChange` lets it detect file changes at runtime.
JsonFile.When1: Use `JsonFileStore` when the translations are deployed as files next to the application: ASP.NET Core sites and APIs, worker services, console and desktop programs. The files can be corrected or replaced without recompiling, and with `ReloadOnChange` even without restarting. It supports every file name of the [JSON store family](docs/stores/json#namespaces), namespace files included.
JsonFile.Browser: `JsonFileStore` needs a file system, so it does not work in the browser: in Blazor WebAssembly its constructor throws `PlatformNotSupportedException`, and the compiler's platform analyzer warns about it. Use `EmbeddedJsonStore` or `HttpJsonStore` there.
JsonFile.Setup1: Put the catalogs in a folder of the project, by default `Locales`:
JsonFile.Setup2: The store reads the files from the folder of the *running* application, not from the project folder. The package does not add build rules to your project, so add these lines to the `.csproj` to copy the files when building and publishing:
JsonFile.Setup3: Then create the store, once, at startup:
JsonFile.OptPath: The folder that contains the catalogs. A relative path starts from the application folder (`AppContext.BaseDirectory`, where the application's `.dll` is), *not* from the current working directory, so the store finds its files wherever the program is started from. Absolute paths are allowed.
JsonFile.OptReload: Watches the folder and applies changes to the files while the application runs. See [Reloading files](docs/stores/json/file#reload).
JsonFile.FilesTitle: How files are found and read
JsonFile.Files1: The store works in two phases:
JsonFile.FilesIndex: *When it is created*, it lists every `*.json` file in `ResourcesPath` and in its subfolders, and works out the culture of each one from its name. It does not read the files yet. If the folder does not exist, the store simply has no files (or throws, with `ThrowOnMissingStore`).
JsonFile.FilesNames: A file belongs to a culture when its name is `'{culture}.json'`, `'{culture}.{namespace}.json'` or `'{namespace}.{culture}.json'`, or when it sits in a folder named after the culture (`'{culture}'/…json`). Other files are ignored, unless `FileMappings` points to them.
JsonFile.FilesLazy: *On each lookup*, it reads and parses a file the first time a key needs it, and keeps the parsed content in memory. Later lookups in the same file read nothing from disk.
JsonFile.FilesStrict: With `ThrowOnMissingStore = true`, the store instead reads and checks every file when it is created, so a broken file stops the application at startup.
JsonFile.Reload1: With `ReloadOnChange = true`, the store watches its folder and subfolders with a `FileSystemWatcher`:
JsonFile.ReloadEvents: A changed file is read again on its next use. New, deleted and renamed files are added to or removed from the list at once, so a new language or namespace becomes available without restarting. If the watcher reports an error, the store scans the folder again and forgets everything it had read.
JsonFile.ReloadRendered: Text already resolved, such as a page already rendered, does not change by itself: the next request uses the new text.
JsonFile.ReloadFolder: If the folder does not exist, the store creates it in order to watch it.
JsonFile.ReloadLimits: File-system notifications are not delivered reliably on every system: some network shares and container volumes do not report changes. Reloading is a convenience for development and for corrections, not a synchronization mechanism.
JsonFile.ReloadDispose: The watcher stays active until the store is disposed of: use `using`, or create the store with a factory in [dependency injection](docs/dependency-injection#store), which disposes of it when the application stops.
JsonFile.ErrPlatform: The store is created in a browser application.
JsonFile.ErrMapping: A `FileMappings` value is not a valid relative `.json` path inside the folder.
JsonFile.ErrNotFound: With `ThrowOnMissingStore = true`: the directory is missing or contains no `.json` files at construction, or neither the requested culture nor the fallback has files during lookup. Regardless of the option: only other regional variants of the same language have files for the requested culture or fallback.
JsonFile.ErrJson: With `ThrowOnMissingStore = true`: a file is not valid JSON. Without it, the file is ignored.
JsonFile.ErrSize: A file is larger than `MaxDocumentBytes`, whatever the value of `ThrowOnMissingStore`.
JsonFile.ErrSecurity: The folder, or a file to read, is a symbolic link or another reparse point, or a path would leave the folder.
JsonFile.Errors2: Without `ThrowOnMissingStore`, files that cannot be read (because they are locked or access is denied) are skipped like invalid ones. All these exceptions reach the caller of `Resolve()` unchanged.
JsonFile.Security1: The store refuses symbolic links and other reparse points, both for the folder and for every file it reads, and never builds a path outside `ResourcesPath`. Keep the folder writable only by the account that deploys the application: a check on the path cannot rule out a link created between the check and the read.
JsonFile.Example1: A console program with every option set. While it runs, edit `it.json` in the output folder and press Enter: the new text appears without restarting.

JsonEmbedded.Title: EmbeddedJsonStore
JsonEmbedded.Description: Loads JSON catalogs included in the assembly as embedded resources. Translations ship with the binary, including in Blazor WebAssembly, without separate catalog files.
JsonEmbedded.When1: `EmbeddedJsonStore` reads catalogs that the compiler has packed inside a `.dll`, as *embedded resources*. The translations travel with the binary and cannot get lost or out of sync. It is the right choice for:
JsonEmbedded.WhenLibrary: *libraries* that ship their own texts in their NuGet package;
JsonEmbedded.WhenSingleFile: *single-file and self-contained applications*, where extra files are inconvenient;
JsonEmbedded.WhenBrowser: *Blazor WebAssembly applications with small catalogs*: the translations are downloaded with the application, and `Resolve()` works from the first render. This site uses it.
JsonEmbedded.When2: Updating a translation requires rebuilding and redeploying the assembly. The store also loads every catalog into memory, even if the application uses only one language.
JsonEmbedded.Setup1: Mark the catalogs as embedded resources in the `.csproj` of the project that contains them:
JsonEmbedded.Setup2: Then create the store, once, at startup. It reads every catalog immediately, in the constructor:
JsonEmbedded.SetupAssembly: Always set `ResourceAssembly`. By default the store reads the *entry* assembly, the one of the program that was started: in a unit test that is the test runner, and in a plugin it is the host application, not the assembly that contains your files.
JsonEmbedded.OptAssembly: The assembly that contains the catalogs. When `null`, the store uses `Assembly.GetEntryAssembly()`, and if there is none, the assembly of the store itself, which contains no catalogs.
JsonEmbedded.OptPath: The folder of the catalogs inside the project, used to select resources by name. It is not a disk path: `/` and `\` are converted to `.` to match resource names. An empty value selects every `.json` resource of the assembly.
JsonEmbedded.OptShared: Inherited from `JsonStoreSettings`: see [Shared settings](docs/stores/json#settings). In `FileMappings`, the value is a file name alone, such as `it-IT.json`.
JsonEmbedded.NamesTitle: How resources are named and matched
JsonEmbedded.Names1: The compiler gives each embedded file a *resource name* made of the project's root namespace, the folders and the file name, joined by dots. The store relies on those names:
JsonEmbedded.NamesSelect: It selects the resources whose name ends in `.json` and contains `ResourcesPath` as a segment: `Locales.` at the start or `.Locales.` in the middle, ignoring case.
JsonEmbedded.NamesCulture: It identifies each catalog by the last part of its name before `.json`: `MyCompany.MyApp.Locales.it-IT.json` becomes `it-IT.json`, the culture file of `it-IT`.
JsonEmbedded.NamesUnique: So subfolders are allowed but do not count, and two files with the same final name, in different folders, overwrite each other. Namespace files are not supported: `it.common.json` is read as `common.json`, which no culture uses.
JsonEmbedded.NamesFolders: MSBuild changes some characters in *folder* names when it builds resource names (a `-` or a space becomes `_`). Keep the folder name simple, such as `Locales`, so that `ResourcesPath` matches it.
JsonEmbedded.SatelliteWarning: Never embed a file whose name ends with a culture before `.json`, such as `common.it-IT.json` or `Strings.fr.json`. MSBuild recognizes the culture and moves the file to a separate *satellite assembly*, which the store does not read: the file silently disappears. Culture files such as `it-IT.json` are not affected.
JsonEmbedded.Names2: To check which resources an assembly contains, list their names:
JsonEmbedded.Culture1: The store does not know in advance which cultures exist. For a request in `it-CH` it tries, in order, and returns the first text it finds:
JsonEmbedded.CultureStep1: the file mapped to `it-CH` in `FileMappings`, then `it-CH.json`;
JsonEmbedded.CultureStep3: the same files for `FallbackCulture` and its language.
JsonEmbedded.Culture2: A neutral request never discovers a regional file: an `it` request does not read `it-IT.json`. Name each language's main catalog after the neutral culture, as in the [recommended layout](docs/stores/json#layout). The store never throws because only a regional variant of the same language exists: it moves on to the fallback.
JsonEmbedded.LoadingStartup: The constructor reads and parses every selected resource, so all languages are in memory from the start and lookups never touch the assembly again.
JsonEmbedded.LoadingCache: The most recently found templates, up to 512 combinations of key and culture, are also remembered to make repeated lookups faster. Missing keys are not remembered.
JsonEmbedded.LoadingThreads: The store is thread-safe: create one and share it.
JsonEmbedded.LoadingDispose: `EmbeddedJsonStore` does not keep file handles or other disposable resources open and does not implement `IDisposable`. A declaration such as `using var store = new EmbeddedJsonStore(…)` does not compile.
JsonEmbedded.ErrNotFound: With `ThrowOnMissingStore = true`: no resource matches `ResourcesPath` (when the store is created), or neither the culture nor the fallback has a catalog (on lookup).
JsonEmbedded.ErrJson: With `ThrowOnMissingStore = true`: a resource is not valid JSON, when the store is created. Without it, the resource is skipped.
JsonEmbedded.ErrSize: A resource is larger than `MaxDocumentBytes`, when the store is created, whatever the value of `ThrowOnMissingStore`.
JsonEmbedded.Example1: This site is a Blazor WebAssembly application that shows every page in five languages. Its catalogs are `Locales/en.json`, `it.json`, `fr.json`, `de.json` and `es.json`, embedded in the application:
JsonEmbedded.Example2: `ThrowOnMissingStore` turns a packaging mistake into an error at startup instead of a site full of placeholders. Because the catalogs are in memory, the components render with `Resolve()` and the language changes instantly, without any download.

JsonHttp.Title: HttpJsonStore
JsonHttp.Description: `HttpJsonStore` downloads JSON catalogs on demand and caches them in memory. Use it in Blazor WebAssembly or other clients that load translations at runtime.
JsonHttp.When1: `HttpJsonStore` reads the same catalogs as the other JSON stores, but from a web server, through an `HttpClient`. Choose it when:
JsonHttp.WhenSize: the catalogs are large, and downloading only the languages and the sections in use makes the application start faster;
JsonHttp.WhenUpdate: translations must be corrected without publishing a new version of the application: replace the files on the server, and the store can check for changes with `RefreshStoreAsync()`;
JsonHttp.WhenClients: the application runs in the browser (Blazor WebAssembly) or is a client that gets its content from a server.
JsonHttp.Setup1: Publish the catalogs as static files. In a Blazor WebAssembly or ASP.NET Core project, put them under `wwwroot`, for example in `wwwroot/locales`:
JsonHttp.Setup2: Then give the store an `HttpClient` whose `BaseAddress` is the address of the site. The store requests each file at `'{BaseAddress}{ResourcesPath}/{file}'`:
JsonHttp.BaseAddress: End `BaseAddress` with `/`. Relative addresses are resolved like links in a web page: with `https://example.com/myapp` (no final slash) the store requests `https://example.com/locales/en.json`, outside your application, and every file appears to be missing. In Blazor, `builder.HostEnvironment.BaseAddress` already ends with `/`.
JsonHttp.Setup3: Creating the store does not download anything: the first request happens when a translation or a preload needs it.
JsonHttp.OptPath: The URL path of the catalogs, relative to `BaseAddress`. Note the lowercase default, unlike the other stores. It must be a relative path: a leading `/`, `.` or `..` segments, `\`, `:`, `?`, `#` and `%` are rejected with `ArgumentException` when the store is created. An empty value means the catalogs are directly at `BaseAddress`. Each part is URL-encoded when the request is built.
JsonHttp.OptShared: Inherited from `JsonStoreSettings`: see [Shared settings](docs/stores/json#settings). For HTTP, invalid JSON and failed requests always throw, whatever the value of `ThrowOnMissingStore`.
JsonHttp.LoadingTitle: Loading: on demand or up front
JsonHttp.Loading1: The store keeps in memory every file it has downloaded. A file is requested once; a file that turned out to be missing (`404`) is remembered too, and not requested again. There are two ways to fill the memory:
JsonHttp.Lazy: `ResolveAsync()` downloads the files the key needs: first the list of files, if there is a manifest, then the candidate files of the culture one by one until one contains the key, and the fallback culture's files only if the key was not found. The next lookups for the same files need no network:
JsonHttp.Preload1: `LoadAsync` downloads the catalogs of one or more cultures, and of the fallback culture, in advance:
JsonHttp.PreloadFallback: The fallback culture is always loaded too, so that synchronous lookups can fall back.
JsonHttp.PreloadWhat: Without a manifest, it loads the culture files only: the mapped file, `it-CH.json` and `it.json` for `it-CH`. Namespace files are loaded later, on demand. With a manifest, it loads every file listed for the culture that best matches the request, namespace files included, plus the files listed for its neutral culture, such as `it.json` for `it-CH`.
JsonHttp.PreloadSync: After `LoadAsync`, `Resolve()` works without network access, which is what Razor rendering needs.
JsonHttp.PreloadSwitch: Call it again, and wait for it, before switching to another language.
JsonHttp.SyncWarning: `Resolve()` never downloads. If the request's culture, or the fallback culture when the key is not found, has not been loaded yet, it throws `InvalidOperationException`. Without a manifest, a key that exists only in a namespace file that has not been downloaded yet is reported as missing: preload with a manifest, or use `ResolveAsync()`.
JsonHttp.Manifest1: `manifest.json` is an optional file, placed next to the catalogs, that lists them. It is a JSON array of paths relative to `ResourcesPath`:
JsonHttp.RequestsWithout: Every possible file name is tried; each file that does not exist costs a request answered with `404`.
JsonHttp.PreloadWith: Every listed file of the culture and of its neutral culture, namespaces included.
JsonHttp.RegionalWithout: File names are guessed: `it` never finds `it-IT.json`.
JsonHttp.RegionalWith: The list is known: `it` finds `it-IT.json` (see [culture matching](docs/stores/json#culture)).
JsonHttp.ManifestFormat: Each entry must be a text with a relative `.json` path that stays inside `ResourcesPath`. Anything else (another type of value, an absolute path, `..`, `%`) makes the manifest invalid and throws `JsonException` or `ArgumentException`.
JsonHttp.ManifestOnly: With a manifest, files that are not listed are never requested. Keep it in sync with the files, ideally by generating it in the build.
JsonHttp.ManifestOnce: The store requests the manifest once, before the first catalog. If the server answers `404`, the store works without a manifest.
JsonHttp.ManifestSync: Files listed in the manifest follow the same name rules as the files on disk, and the same [fallback order](docs/stores/json#fallback).
JsonHttp.Requests1: Without a manifest, the store has to try file names. For the key `checkout:Title` in `it-CH`, on a server that has only `en.json`, `it.json` and `it.checkout.json`, the first `ResolveAsync()` sends:
JsonHttp.Requests2: The store remembers `404` responses and does not repeat requests for those file names. A manifest avoids these exploratory requests and is recommended in production.
JsonHttp.Refresh1: `RefreshStoreAsync()` checks the server for newer versions of the manifest and of every file already downloaded:
JsonHttp.RefreshConditional: Sends `Cache-Control: no-cache`, with `If-None-Match` and `If-Modified-Since` when the server supplied an `ETag` or `Last-Modified` value. A `304 Not Modified` response keeps the in-memory copy without downloading the content again.
JsonHttp.RefreshAtomic: The new versions replace the old ones all together, only after every response has been received and parsed. If anything fails, the previous versions stay in use and the exception is thrown to the caller. Lookups made during a refresh keep working with the previous versions.
JsonHttp.RefreshManual: Refresh is explicit: call the method when your application needs it, for example from a timer or a button handler.
JsonHttp.RefreshRender: Text already rendered does not change: render the components again after the refresh.
JsonHttp.Caching1: The store receives files through the normal HTTP stack, so browser caches, CDNs and `Cache-Control` headers apply as usual. Choose the cache headers on the server according to how often translations change.
JsonHttp.Caching2: Keep the files as ordinary JSON and let the server compress them with gzip or Brotli (`Content-Encoding`). In the browser, decompression is automatic. On desktop and server .NET, enable `AutomaticDecompression` on the `HttpClientHandler` of the client you pass to the store; this property is not supported in WebAssembly.
JsonHttp.ErrNull: The `HttpClient`, or a culture passed to `LoadAsync` or to a lookup, is `null`.
JsonHttp.ErrPath: `ResourcesPath`, a `FileMappings` value or a manifest entry is not a valid relative path (when the store is created, or when the manifest is read).
JsonHttp.ErrNotLoaded: `Resolve()` needs a culture that has not been loaded. See the warning above.
JsonHttp.ErrHttp: The server answers with an error other than `404`, a response is larger than `MaxDocumentBytes`, or the server answers `304` to a request that was not conditional. Always, regardless of `ThrowOnMissingStore`.
JsonHttp.ErrJson: A catalog or the manifest is not valid JSON, or the manifest is not an array of paths. Always.
JsonHttp.ErrNotFound: With `ThrowOnMissingStore = true`: neither the culture nor the fallback has any file. Always: only a regional variant of the same language exists, as described in [culture matching](docs/stores/json#culture).
JsonHttp.ErrCanceled: The `CancellationToken` passed to `LoadAsync`, `ResolveAsync` or `RefreshStoreAsync` is canceled.
JsonHttp.Errors2: A `404` is never an error: it only means that the file does not exist. These exceptions are not converted by the translator: they reach the caller of `Resolve()`, `ResolveAsync()` or of the store's methods.
JsonHttp.LifetimeShare: Create one store for the application and share it; it is thread-safe. Concurrent requests that need the same culture wait for a single download.
JsonHttp.LifetimeClient: The caller manages the `HttpClient` lifetime. Disposing the store releases only its internal locks; it does not dispose the client.
JsonHttp.LifetimeThreads: Register the store itself in dependency injection as well, as in the example below, if components need to call `LoadAsync` or `RefreshStoreAsync`.
JsonHttp.Example1: A complete `Program.cs` that preloads the user's language before the first render, and a component that switches language:
JsonHttp.Example2: Components that show text must render again after the switch: the button's own component does so after its event handler, and other components can receive the culture as a cascading value. The repository's [Blazor sample](https://github.com/berik-99/FluentLocalizer/tree/main/Examples/FluentLocalizer.Samples.BlazorWebApp) shows manifest preloading, on-demand namespaces and refresh in a running application.

CustomStore.Title: Custom stores
CustomStore.Description: Implement the two `ITranslationStore` methods to retrieve templates from a database, CMS or external service. The translator continues to handle message formatting.
CustomStore.Contract1: A store is any class that implements `ITranslationStore`, from the core package:
CustomStore.RuleRaw: *Return the raw template*, exactly as written, without filling in values: the translator formats it.
CustomStore.RuleMissing: *Return `null` when there is no template* for the key. Throwing `KeyNotFoundException` is also understood as a missing translation; any other exception is not.
CustomStore.RuleFallback: *Apply your own culture fallback*. The translator passes the culture of the request and does not try other cultures by itself: if `it-CH` should fall back to `it` and then to English, the store does it.
CustomStore.RuleSync: *Never block in `GetTemplate`*. The synchronous method must answer from data already in memory: waiting for a database or a download with `.Result` or `.Wait()` can freeze a user interface or exhaust a server's threads. If the data is not loaded yet, load it in advance (as below) or throw `InvalidOperationException`, as `HttpJsonStore` does.
CustomStore.RuleThreads: *Make the store thread-safe*. The application shares one store, so it must support concurrent requests.
CustomStore.RuleErrors: *Throw only for real failures*. Exceptions other than `KeyNotFoundException` reach the caller of `Resolve()` unchanged, so reserve them for problems that should stop the operation, such as an unreachable database.
CustomStore.Dictionary1: This store keeps the templates in dictionaries grouped by culture, and walks from the requested culture to its parents (`it-CH`, then `it`) before trying a default language:
CustomStore.Dictionary2: `CultureInfo.Parent` gives the next, more general culture: `it-CH` → `it` → the invariant culture, whose name is empty. The same loop works for any culture.
CustomStore.DatabaseTitle: Example: preload templates from a database
CustomStore.Database1: If templates are stored in a database, load them at startup and keep them in memory so both lookup methods can respond without database access. Call `LoadAsync` again when you need to refresh the data:
CustomStore.Database2: The function that reads the rows is passed in, so the store works with Entity Framework, Dapper, a REST API or a file. The new dictionary is built separately and swapped in a single assignment, so concurrent lookups always see either the old or the new catalog, never half of each.
CustomStore.Combining1: Because every store has the same interface, stores can wrap other stores. This one asks a second store only when the first has no template, for example to let local files override the catalogs shipped with the application:
CustomStore.Combining2: The first store applies its own fallback before answering: a `JsonFileStore` with English as fallback returns the English text rather than `null`, so the second store is asked only for keys that the first does not know in any language.
CustomStore.JsonBase1: If your source provides whole JSON documents, for example one per culture stored in a database, derive from `JsonTranslationStoreBase`. It is the base class of `JsonFileStore` and `EmbeddedJsonStore`, and gives you the JSON parsing, nested keys, culture fallback and template cache of the family. Its protected members:
CustomStore.MemberOptions: The `JsonStoreSettings` passed to the constructor: fallback culture, mappings, and so on.
CustomStore.MemberSet: Parses a JSON text, or copies a parsed element, and stores it under a file name such as `it.json` or `en-US.json`. A document with the same name is replaced.
CustomStore.MemberClear: Empties the cache of templates already found. Call it after changing documents.
CustomStore.MemberCandidates: The file names tried for a culture, in fallback order: the mapped file, the culture, its language, then the same for the fallback culture.
CustomStore.MemberFind: Looks up the key in stored documents in candidate order. Override this method to customize the lookup.
CustomStore.MemberHas: Checks whether a candidate document exists for the culture. Used by `ThrowOnMissingStore`; the method can be overridden.
CustomStore.MemberGet: Public methods that can be overridden. `GetTemplate` uses the cache and `FindTemplate`; `GetTemplateAsync` delegates to `GetTemplate`.
CustomStore.JsonBaseCache: `SetDocument` and `RemoveDocument` do not empty the template cache. Without `ClearTemplateCache()`, keys already found keep returning their previous text.
CustomStore.Register1: A custom store is used exactly like the built-in ones: pass it to `new Translator(store)`, or register it with dependency injection:
CustomStore.Check1: `GetTemplate` answers from memory and never waits for I/O.
CustomStore.Check3: Culture fallback is applied inside the store.
CustomStore.Check4: Concurrent calls from several threads are safe.
CustomStore.Check5: If the store holds resources (connections, watchers, timers), it implements `IDisposable`.

Migration.Title: Versions and migration
Migration.Description: Review the changes in each release and the updates needed to migrate code from an earlier version.
Migration.Versions1: The three packages are always released together, with the same version number:
Migration.Version100: First stable release. The public API and the behavior are the same as in `0.1.0-alpha`.
Migration.Version010: The three dedicated JSON stores (`JsonFileStore`, `EmbeddedJsonStore`, `HttpJsonStore`) and their shared settings. New namespaces, editable `TranslationOptions`, corrected dependency injection registration. `JsonStore` becomes a deprecated wrapper.
Migration.Version001: First release: translator, fluent builder, options, logging, the mode-based `JsonStore` and the dependency injection extensions.
Migration.Versions2: The [API reference](docs/api) can show any of these versions and lists, for each one, what was added, changed, deprecated and removed.
Migration.From0011: Version `0.1.0-alpha` contains breaking changes. Code written for `0.0.1` needs the following updates.
Migration.Namespaces: The core types moved from `FluentLocalizer.Core` to `FluentLocalizer`, and the logging types from `FluentLocalizer.Core.Logging` to `FluentLocalizer.Logging`. Update the `using` directives and any fully qualified names. Only `FluentLocalizerBuilder`, in the dependency injection package, still lives in `FluentLocalizer.Core`.
Migration.JsonStoreTitle: From JsonStore to the dedicated stores
Migration.JsonStore1: `JsonStore` chose between the file system and embedded resources with an option. Each source now has its own store and its own options class:
Migration.Options: The properties of `TranslationOptions` used `init` accessors and could only be set when the object was created. They now have normal `set` accessors, so they can also be configured in a dependency injection callback. Existing object initializers keep compiling.
Migration.Injection: `AddFluentLocalizer(services, options)` now really registers the options object you pass, and both overloads validate their arguments against `null`. `WithStore(store)` no longer registers the store twice. No code change is needed, but behavior that relied on the old registrations may differ.
Migration.FromHttp: The HTTP store used to be a separate package. It is now part of `FluentLocalizer.Store.Json`: replace the package reference and change `using FluentLocalizer.Store.Http;` to `using FluentLocalizer.Store.Json;`. `HttpJsonStore` and `HttpJsonStoreOptions` keep their names.
Migration.Deprecated1: `JsonStore`, `JsonStoreOptions` and `JsonStoreLocation` are marked `[Obsolete]` and produce a compiler warning. They still work, so existing applications keep running while they migrate:
Migration.DeprecatedWrapper: `JsonStore` creates a `JsonFileStore` or an `EmbeddedJsonStore` with the same settings and forwards every lookup to it, so it follows the rules of the dedicated stores. For example, files on disk are now read the first time they are needed, instead of all at once when the store is created.
Migration.DeprecatedMax: It does not pass on `MaxDocumentBytes`: with `JsonStore` the size limit is never applied.
Migration.DeprecatedBrowser: With `SearchMode = FileSystem` (the default) it throws `PlatformNotSupportedException` in the browser, like `JsonFileStore`.
Migration.Reference1: Every type and member of the [API reference](docs/api) shows the version that introduced it, and deprecated members name their replacement. Each package's README on [GitHub](https://github.com/berik-99/FluentLocalizer) contains the same reference for the latest version.
